title: Conclusion
text:
Across five weeks of analysis, the computational evidence consistently supports the central claim of this portfolio: Minimal Tech House and Hard House are measurably distinct genres, not just different labels for similar music.
At the corpus level (Week 8), the two genres occupy clearly different regions of Spotify’s feature space. Energy, tempo, and loudness all separate them cleanly, and the chroma analysis of East Bridge Romance showed that even within a single Hard House track, form emerges from textural contrast around a narrow harmonic core rather than from harmonic complexity.
Looking at individual track structure (Week 9), the self-similarity matrices revealed that chroma and timbre capture fundamentally different dimensions. A track can repeat the same chords throughout while still evolving texturally, a distinction that would be invisible in a purely harmonic analysis. The keygram analysis (Week 10) reinforced this: EDM tracks like Wood maintain a stable key with no modulation, reflecting a compositional philosophy built on repetition rather than development.
At the rhythmic level (Week 11), Hard House maintains a rigid, unwavering beat, while Minimal Tech House distributes its rhythmic energy more diffusely. The tempograms and novelty functions make this contrast visually and numerically concrete.
The classification and clustering analysis (Week 12) tied everything together. A random forest classifier achieved approximately 99.5% accuracy with 10-fold cross-validation, and a reduced model using only five features performed equally well. Hierarchical clustering recovered the genre boundary without any labels, validating the supervised results through an independent, unsupervised approach.

title: Conclusion
text:
Who Could Benefit
These findings are relevant for several audiences. DJs and curators could apply similar feature-based approaches to sort large music libraries, identify tracks that bridge genres, or discover unexpected overlaps between playlists. Music producers gain concrete insight into which measurable properties define genre identity, helping them position their tracks within or across genre boundaries. Researchers in Music Information Retrieval can see how standard Spotify features perform on a focused, two-genre classification task, and importantly, where those features fall short. Spotify’s features say nothing about arrangement, mixing technique, sound design, or cultural context, all of which are central to how listeners and practitioners actually experience these genres.

title: Conclusion
text:
What I Learned
Working through this portfolio taught me to approach music analytically without losing sight of what makes it meaningful as a listener and DJ. The course introduced standard MIR tools (chroma features, MFCCs, key estimation, classification) in the context of well-known examples, but applying them to my own corpus required adapting each method to a domain where the differences are more subtle than, say, comparing classical music to pop.
One example of this is the reduced-model experiment in Week 12. The course covered random forests and feature importance as general tools, but I independently decided to test whether a minimal subset of features could match the full model’s accuracy. The result (five features performing as well as ten) was not something the course explicitly demonstrated, and it gave me a concrete answer to the question of which features actually matter for this genre pair.
Similarly, combining supervised and unsupervised methods on the same data was my own decision. The course taught each technique separately, but applying both to the same corpus and comparing the results (the classifier’s near-perfect accuracy and the dendrogram’s clean two-branch structure) provided a form of converging evidence that neither method could offer alone. This kind of methodological triangulation is something I now see as essential for drawing credible conclusions from computational analyses.

title: Conclusion
text:
Limitations & Future Work
This analysis relies entirely on Spotify’s proprietary audio features and on chroma and timbre exports from Sonic Visualiser. Both are approximations. Spotify’s features are black-box estimates that may not correspond to perceptual or musicological categories, and the Sonic Visualiser exports depend on algorithm-specific assumptions about tuning, windowing, and spectral resolution.
The corpus itself is limited to two curated playlists, meaning that the results reflect these particular selections rather than the genres as a whole. A track that appears in one playlist but not another might change the analysis. Future work could expand the corpus to include multiple playlists from different curators, incorporate additional analytical methods like structural segmentation or harmonic rhythm analysis, or apply the same methodology to genre pairs where the distinction is less clearcut.
Despite these limitations, the consistency of results across five independent analysis methods (feature distributions, self-similarity, tonal analysis, temporal analysis, and machine learning) provides strong converging evidence. What the body feels on the dance floor, the difference between swaying and jumping, has a computational signature. The machine can hear it too.

title: Week 11: Tempo & Rhythm
text: Tempo is one of the most immediate perceptual differences between Minimal Tech House and Hard House. This section combines corpus-level analysis (tempo distribution) with track-level analysis (novelty functions and tempograms) to examine how rhythmic pacing and pulse stability differ between the two genres.

title: Week 11: Tempo & Rhythm
text: Tempo is one of the most immediate perceptual differences between Minimal Tech House and Hard House. This section combines corpus-level analysis (tempo distribution) with track-level analysis (novelty functions and tempograms) to examine how rhythmic pacing and pulse stability differ between the two genres.

title: Week 11: Tempo & Rhythm
text:
Corpus Tempo Distribution
A histogram with 2 BPM bins compares the tempo distribution across both genres using overlaid bars. This approach reveals not just the central tendency but the full distributional shape, including overlap zones and bimodality.


Histogram: tempo distribution per genre
# Overlaid histogram with 2 BPM bins to compare tempo distributions
# position = "identity" overlays rather than stacks the bars
ggplot(corpus, aes(x = Tempo, fill = Genre)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, alpha = 0.5, position = "identity") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pal) +
  theme_freq(12) +
  labs(
    title = "Tempo Distribution Across the Corpus",
    subtitle = "Each bar = 2 BPM | 861 tracks",
    x = "Tempo (BPM)", y = "Number of Tracks", fill = NULL
  )









The histogram confirms that tempo is one of the strongest differentiators between the two genres. Hard House clusters sharply around 138–150 BPM, reflecting the genre’s aggressive, high-energy character. Minimal Tech House concentrates around 120–128 BPM, which is the classic house tempo range associated with groove-oriented, danceable rhythms. The two distributions barely overlap, with a near-empty zone between 128 and 138 BPM functioning as a natural boundary. Tempo alone could serve as a reasonably effective genre predictor for these two subgenres.

title: Week 11: Tempo & Rhythm
text:
Novelty Functions: First 60 Seconds
Novelty functions are computed by Sonic Visualiser and measure the spectral flux (rate of change) in the audio signal over time. Peaks correspond to rhythmic onsets. Two representative tracks are compared in a faceted line plot.


Novelty functions: spectral flux over time
# Load novelty curves exported from Sonic Visualiser
# Columns: TIME (seconds), VALUE (spectral flux magnitude)
hard_nov <- read_csv("mytrack-novelty.csv", col_names = c("TIME", "VALUE"),
  show_col_types = FALSE) |> mutate(Genre = "Hard House: It Ain't Over")
min_nov <- read_csv("minimal-novelty.csv", col_names = c("TIME", "VALUE"),
  show_col_types = FALSE) |> mutate(Genre = "Minimal Tech House: Overflow (Kolter)")

# Faceted line plot comparing the first 60 seconds of each track
bind_rows(hard_nov, min_nov) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = TIME, y = VALUE, colour = Genre)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.8, linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Hard House: It Ain't Over" = "#ff2d55",
    "Minimal Tech House: Overflow (Kolter)" = "#00d4ff")) +
  facet_wrap(~Genre, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  xlim(0, 60) +
  theme_freq(11) +
  labs(
    title = "Novelty Functions: It Ain't Over vs Overflow",
    subtitle = "Onset strength over the first 60 seconds",
    x = "Time (s)", y = "Novelty", colour = NULL
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")









The novelty functions capture how abruptly the spectral content changes over time, which closely tracks rhythmic onsets. Hard House (It Ain’t Over) shows a pattern of sharp, evenly-spaced peaks with high amplitude, a direct reflection of its relentless four-on-the-floor kick drum pattern where every beat hits hard. Minimal Tech House (Overflow) shows a more irregular pattern with lower peak amplitude, consistent with its approach of gradual, texture-based development where rhythmic elements are layered subtly rather than delivered with force.

title: Week 11: Tempo & Rhythm
text:
Tempograms: Hard House (It Ain’t Over)
Tempograms visualise how rhythmic energy is distributed across different tempo frequencies over time. The ACT (autocorrelation) method detects periodicity in the onset signal, while the DFT (Fourier) method captures harmonic structure in the rhythm. Both are rendered as heatmaps using geom_raster.

ACTDFT




ACT tempogram: Hard House
# Load ACT tempogram data and reshape from wide to long format
# Reciprocal y-axis transforms lag values to BPM
read_csv("mytrack-act.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  pivot_longer(-TIME, names_to = "tempo") |>
  mutate(tempo = as.numeric(tempo)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = TIME, y = tempo, fill = value)) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_y_continuous(transform = c("reciprocal", "reverse"), breaks = seq(50, 350, 50)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(guide = "none") +
  theme_freq(11) + theme(panel.grid = element_blank()) +
  labs(title = "ACT Tempogram: It Ain't Over (Hard House)", x = "Time (s)", y = "Tempo (BPM)")













DFT tempogram: Hard House
# DFT tempogram captures harmonic structure in the rhythm
read_csv("mytrack-dft.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  pivot_longer(-TIME, names_to = "tempo") |>
  mutate(tempo = as.numeric(tempo)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = TIME, y = tempo, fill = value)) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(guide = "none") +
  theme_freq(11) + theme(panel.grid = element_blank()) +
  labs(title = "DFT Tempogram: It Ain't Over (Hard House)", x = "Time (s)", y = "Tempo (BPM)")

title: Week 11: Tempo & Rhythm
text:
Tempograms: Minimal Tech House (Overflow)

ACTDFT




ACT tempogram: Minimal Tech House
read_csv("minimal-act.csv",show_col_types=F)|>pivot_longer(-TIME,names_to="tempo")|>mutate(tempo=as.numeric(tempo))|>
  ggplot(aes(x=TIME,y=tempo,fill=value))+geom_raster()+scale_y_continuous(transform=c("reciprocal","reverse"),breaks=seq(50,350,50))+
  scale_fill_viridis_c(guide="none")+theme_freq(11)+theme(panel.grid=element_blank())+labs(title="ACT Tempogram: Overflow (Minimal Tech House)",x="Time (s)",y="Tempo (BPM)")













DFT tempogram: Minimal Tech House
read_csv("minimal-dft.csv",show_col_types=F)|>pivot_longer(-TIME,names_to="tempo")|>mutate(tempo=as.numeric(tempo))|>
  ggplot(aes(x=TIME,y=tempo,fill=value))+geom_raster()+scale_fill_viridis_c(guide="none")+
  theme_freq(11)+theme(panel.grid=element_blank())+labs(title="DFT Tempogram: Overflow (Minimal Tech House)",x="Time (s)",y="Tempo (BPM)")













Interpretation
The tempograms complement the novelty analysis by showing how rhythmic energy is distributed across tempo frequencies over time. The Hard House ACT tempogram displays a strong, consistent horizontal band at the track’s tempo, pointing to a metrically rigid, unwavering beat. The DFT tempogram reveals additional energy at integer multiples and sub-multiples of the main tempo, harmonic artifacts that reflect the regularity of the pulse. For Minimal Tech House, the energy distribution is noticeably more diffuse: the rhythmic pulse is present but less forcefully articulated, consistent with a genre that favours subtlety over impact.
Together with the self-similarity analysis from Week 9, these tempograms complete the picture. Both genres are loop-based and repetitive, but Hard House asserts this through rhythmic rigidity, while Minimal Tech House expresses it through gradual textural continuity.

title: Week 9: Self-Similarity & Timbre
text: A Self-Similarity Matrix (SSM) compares every moment in a track with every other moment, producing a visual map of structural repetition and contrast. By computing SSMs from both chroma (harmonic) and timbre (textural) features, we can examine whether a track’s form is driven by harmonic development or by changes in sound texture. The SSMs below were computed from Sonic Visualiser exports using Euclidean distance on downsampled chroma and MFCC frames.

title: Week 9: Self-Similarity & Timbre
text: A Self-Similarity Matrix (SSM) compares every moment in a track with every other moment, producing a visual map of structural repetition and contrast. By computing SSMs from both chroma (harmonic) and timbre (textural) features, we can examine whether a track’s form is driven by harmonic development or by changes in sound texture. The SSMs below were computed from Sonic Visualiser exports using Euclidean distance on downsampled chroma and MFCC frames.

title: Week 9: Self-Similarity & Timbre
text:
Chroma Self-Similarity: Wood
The chroma SSM for Wood was computed from NNLS Chroma features exported via Sonic Visualiser. The chroma vectors were downsampled (every 50th frame) and the Euclidean distance between all pairs was calculated and plotted as a heatmap.


Chroma SSM: Wood (Euclidean distance)
# Read NNLS Chroma export from Sonic Visualiser
wood <- read_csv("wood.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
chroma_mat <- as.matrix(select(wood, -TIME))

# Downsample: take every 50th frame
idx <- seq(1, nrow(chroma_mat), by = 50)
chroma_small <- chroma_mat[idx, ]
time_w <- wood$TIME[idx]

# Compute pairwise Euclidean distance
dist_w <- as.matrix(dist(chroma_small, method = "euclidean"))

# Prepare data for ggplot
ssm_w <- expand.grid(X = 1:nrow(dist_w), Y = 1:nrow(dist_w))
ssm_w$Distance <- as.vector(dist_w)
ssm_w$TimeX <- time_w[ssm_w$X]
ssm_w$TimeY <- time_w[ssm_w$Y]

ggplot(ssm_w, aes(x = TimeX, y = TimeY, fill = Distance)) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(direction = -1, option = "magma") +
  coord_fixed() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Chroma Self-Similarity Matrix: Wood",
       subtitle = "Calculated using Euclidean distance",
       x = "Time (seconds)", y = "Time (seconds)")





The chroma-based self-similarity matrix of Wood displays a clear block-diagonal structure, with well-defined rectangular regions along the main diagonal. Each block represents a section of the track where harmonic content remains internally consistent, and the sharp transitions between blocks indicate structural boundaries. Wood is composed of discrete, recurring harmonic zones rather than continuous development, which is typical of loop-based electronic music where form emerges through the layering and removal of elements over a repeating harmonic foundation.

title: Week 9: Self-Similarity & Timbre
section: Chroma vs Timbre: Bloed, Zweet en Tranen
text:
Chroma vs Timbre: Bloed, Zweet en Tranen
The same SSM method is applied to Bloed, Zweet en Tranen using both chroma (pitch class) and timbre (MFCC) features. Both SSMs use Euclidean distance on every 50th frame. Comparing the two reveals whether harmonic and timbral structure align or diverge within the same track.

ChromaTimbre




Chroma SSM: Bloed, Zweet en Tranen
# Read NNLS Chroma export from Sonic Visualiser
bzt_pitches <- read_csv("bzt-pitches.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
chroma_mat <- as.matrix(select(bzt_pitches, -TIME))

# Downsample: take every 50th frame
idx_c <- seq(1, nrow(chroma_mat), by = 50)
chroma_small <- chroma_mat[idx_c, ]
time_c <- bzt_pitches$TIME[idx_c]

# Compute pairwise Euclidean distance
dist_c <- as.matrix(dist(chroma_small, method = "euclidean"))

# Prepare data for ggplot
ssm_c <- expand.grid(X = 1:nrow(dist_c), Y = 1:nrow(dist_c))
ssm_c$Distance <- as.vector(dist_c)
ssm_c$TimeX <- time_c[ssm_c$X]
ssm_c$TimeY <- time_c[ssm_c$Y]

ggplot(ssm_c, aes(x = TimeX, y = TimeY, fill = Distance)) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(direction = -1, option = "magma") +
  coord_fixed() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Chroma SSM: Bloed, Zweet en Tranen",
       x = "Time (s)", y = "Time (s)")









Timbre SSM: Bloed, Zweet en Tranen (MFCCs)
# Read MFCC export from Sonic Visualiser (libextract MFCCs)
bzt_timbre <- read_csv("bzt-timbre.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
timbre_mat <- as.matrix(select(bzt_timbre, -TIME))

# Downsample: take every 50th frame
idx_t <- seq(1, nrow(timbre_mat), by = 50)
timbre_small <- timbre_mat[idx_t, ]
time_t <- bzt_timbre$TIME[idx_t]

# Compute pairwise Euclidean distance
dist_t <- as.matrix(dist(timbre_small, method = "euclidean"))

# Prepare data for ggplot
ssm_t <- expand.grid(X = 1:nrow(dist_t), Y = 1:nrow(dist_t))
ssm_t$Distance <- as.vector(dist_t)
ssm_t$TimeX <- time_t[ssm_t$X]
ssm_t$TimeY <- time_t[ssm_t$Y]

ggplot(ssm_t, aes(x = TimeX, y = TimeY, fill = Distance)) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(direction = -1, option = "mako") +
  coord_fixed() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Timbre SSM: Bloed, Zweet en Tranen",
       x = "Time (s)", y = "Time (s)")








Comparing the two SSMs shows that harmonic and timbral structure can diverge significantly within the same track. The chroma SSM has clean, well-defined repetition blocks: the chorus chord progressions return predictably, producing a regular checkerboard-like pattern. The timbre SSM, by contrast, is noisier and more irregular. Even during harmonically identical sections, the texture shifts as vocal intensity varies, drum patterns change, and the arrangement evolves. A track can be harmonically stable while remaining texturally dynamic, and chroma and timbre illuminate fundamentally different dimensions of musical structure. Using only one of these features would give an incomplete picture.

title: Week 9: Self-Similarity & Timbre
text:
Cepstrogram: East Bridge Romance
A cepstrogram visualises the Mel Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCCs) of a track over time. MFCCs capture timbral properties of the audio signal: the first coefficients describe the overall spectral shape (brightness, warmth), while higher coefficients capture finer textural details. Each coefficient is independently scaled to its own range so that variation within each MFCC is visible. This cepstrogram analyses East Bridge Romance, a Hard House track from the corpus, connecting the timbre analysis directly to the chroma analysis in Week 8.


Cepstrogram: East Bridge Romance (MFCCs, per-coefficient scaled)
# Read MFCC data exported from Sonic Visualiser (libextract MFCCs)
eb_timbre <- read_csv("eastbridge-timbre.csv", show_col_types = F)
bin_cols <- paste("BIN", 1:21)

# Downsample for readability (every 5th frame)
eb_ds <- eb_timbre[seq(1, nrow(eb_timbre), by = 5), ]

# Scale each MFCC coefficient independently to 0-1 range
# This ensures all bins contribute equally to the visualisation
eb_scaled <- eb_ds
for (col in bin_cols) {
  vals <- eb_ds[[col]]
  rng <- range(vals, na.rm = TRUE)
  if (rng[2] > rng[1]) {
    eb_scaled[[col]] <- (vals - rng[1]) / (rng[2] - rng[1])
  } else {
    eb_scaled[[col]] <- 0
  }
}

# Pivot to long format for ggplot
eb_long <- eb_scaled |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(bin_cols), names_to = "MFCC", values_to = "Value") |>
  mutate(MFCC = factor(MFCC, levels = rev(bin_cols)))

ggplot(eb_long, aes(x = TIME, y = MFCC, fill = Value)) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(guide = "none") +
  theme_freq(11) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank()) +
  labs(title = "Cepstrogram: East Bridge Romance",
       subtitle = "Per-coefficient scaled MFCCs over time | Hard House",
       x = "Time (s)", y = "")









The cepstrogram of East Bridge Romance reveals how timbral texture evolves across the track. BIN 1 (overall spectral energy) shows clear sectional boundaries that align with the structural transitions visible in the Week 8 chromagram: the drops appear as sudden shifts in lower-order coefficients, while the breakdowns show reduced activity across nearly all bins. Higher-order coefficients (BIN 5 onward) capture finer textural details like the presence of hi-hats, synth textures, and reverb tails. What stands out is that the timbral palette of the track changes more continuously than its harmonic content, reinforcing the observation from the SSM analysis that Hard House structure is driven by textural contrast rather than harmonic development.

text: Computational Musicology (115215146Y) · Universiteit van Amsterdam Instructor: John Ashley Burgoyne

title: Groove vs Aggression
section: Can Machines Hear the Difference Between Groove and Aggression?
text:
Can Machines Hear the Difference Between Groove and Aggression?
This project investigates whether the stylistic contrast between Minimal Tech House and Hard House, two EDM subgenres that share historical roots but occupy opposite ends of the energy spectrum, can be identified and quantified through computational audio features.
Using Spotify’s track-level features, chroma analysis, self-similarity matrices, key profiling, tempograms, and machine learning, we translate subjective genre descriptions like groovy, hypnotic, aggressive, and relentless into measurable musical data.






NoteCentral question



Can the stylistic gap between two EDM subgenres be confirmed through computational evidence, and if so, which features carry the distinction?

title: Groove vs Aggression
text:
The Two Playlists
Minimal Tech House
Groovy Minimal House contains 536 tracks from the intersection of Detroit techno and Chicago house. The genre is defined by restraint: stripped-back percussion, hypnotic basslines, and gradual textural development. Tempos typically sit between 120 and 128 BPM, and energy is sustained but never aggressive. I selected this playlist because it represents the groovy, hypnotic side of electronic music that I personally enjoy as a DJ and listener.
Hard House
Club Heartbroken contains 325 tracks rooted in the UK rave scene. This genre pushes tempo, impact, and emotional intensity to the extreme: 138–150 BPM, aggressive kicks, and maximally compressed masters. I chose this playlist because it sits at the opposite end of the EDM spectrum, favouring maximum intensity over minimal restraint.

title: Groove vs Aggression
text:
Creative Process
As a DJ who plays both minimal and hard sets, I experience the contrast between these genres physically. Minimal Tech House makes you sway; it is music for sustained, hypnotic movement. Hard House makes you jump; it demands immediate, explosive energy. This project tests whether that embodied experience is computationally verifiable. Every analysis in this portfolio asks the same question: can the machine hear what the body already knows?

title: Groove vs Aggression
text:
Assumptions & Limitations
Several assumptions underlie this analysis. Spotify’s audio features are treated as ground truth, but they are black-box estimates. We do not know the exact algorithms behind features like “energy” or “danceability”, and they may not capture what musicians or listeners mean by those terms. Both playlists were curated by individual users and reflect personal taste rather than a systematic sample of either genre. The corpus is also imbalanced (536 vs 325 tracks), which could bias some analyses; the classifier uses stratified cross-validation to mitigate this. Finally, chroma and timbre analyses rely on Sonic Visualiser exports, which use specific algorithms (NNLS Chroma, libextract MFCCs) with their own assumptions about tuning and spectral resolution.
These limitations mean that the conclusions drawn here are indicative rather than definitive. They show what Spotify’s feature space can and cannot capture about these genres, and the confidence in final conclusions is inherently limited by the accuracy of the assumptions described above.

title: Week 8: Track-Level Features
text: This section examines whether the perceived “vibe” of each genre translates into measurable numerical differences. By comparing energy, tempo, loudness, and chroma features across the full corpus, we test whether Spotify’s audio features can capture the contrast between groove-oriented restraint and high-energy aggression.

title: Week 8: Track-Level Features
text:
Energy vs Tempo: Full Corpus
A scatter plot maps each track by its Spotify tempo (x-axis) and energy (y-axis) values, coloured by genre. This visualisation reveals whether the two genres occupy distinct regions of the feature space.


Scatter plot: Energy vs Tempo
# Plot each track as a point in Energy-Tempo space, coloured by genre
# This reveals whether the two genres cluster in different regions
ggplot(corpus, aes(x = Tempo, y = Energy, colour = Genre)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 1.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal) +
  theme_freq(13) +
  labs(
    title = "Minimal Tech House vs Hard House",
    subtitle = "Energy vs Tempo across 861 tracks",
    x = "Tempo (BPM)", y = "Energy", colour = NULL
  )









The scatter plot shows a clear spatial separation between the two genres. Hard House occupies the top-right quadrant, clustering around 138–150 BPM with energy values consistently above 0.8. Minimal Tech House sits in the bottom-left, concentrated between 120–128 BPM with more moderate energy levels. The perceived stylistic contrast is clearly reflected in Spotify’s numerical feature space. The overlap region between the two clusters is small but not empty, which is expected since genres are cultural constructs with fluid edges rather than rigid categories.

title: Week 8: Track-Level Features
text:
Energy, Tempo & Loudness Distributions
Density plots compare the distribution of three key features across both genres, arranged side by side using gridExtra::grid.arrange. Density estimation smooths the raw data into continuous curves, making it easier to compare distributional shapes.


Density plots: Tempo, Energy, Loudness
# Create three density plots comparing key features across genres
# Density estimation smooths raw values into continuous probability curves
p1 <- ggplot(corpus, aes(x = Tempo, fill = Genre)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pal) +
  theme_freq(11) +
  labs(title = "Tempo", x = "BPM", y = "Density", fill = NULL)

p2 <- ggplot(corpus, aes(x = Energy, fill = Genre)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pal) +
  theme_freq(11) +
  labs(title = "Energy", x = "Energy (0-1)", y = "Density", fill = NULL)

p3 <- ggplot(corpus, aes(x = Loudness, fill = Genre)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pal) +
  theme_freq(11) +
  labs(title = "Loudness", x = "Loudness (dB)", y = "Density", fill = NULL)

# Arrange all three side by side for direct comparison
gridExtra::grid.arrange(p1, p2, p3, ncol = 3)









All three density plots show distinct peaks per genre. Tempo provides the cleanest separation, with almost no overlap between 128 and 138 BPM, creating a natural decision boundary. Energy separates well too, though Minimal Tech House shows a wider spread: some tracks push toward higher energy while remaining structurally minimal. Loudness reveals a fundamental difference in mastering philosophy. Hard House peaks around −6 dB (heavily compressed for maximum impact), while Minimal Tech House averages around −10 dB, retaining more dynamic range to create space for the groove to breathe. This 4 dB gap is perceptually significant and reflects a deliberate production choice.

title: Week 8: Track-Level Features
text:
Loudness at the Track Level
To examine the loudness difference in more detail, a combined violin and boxplot compares the full distribution of track-level loudness values across both genres. The violin shape shows the density, while the boxplot inside highlights the median, interquartile range, and outliers.


Violin + boxplot: loudness per genre
ggplot(corpus, aes(x = Genre, y = Loudness, fill = Genre)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.4, colour = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.15, outlier.size = 1, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pal, guide = "none") +
  theme_freq(13) +
  labs(title = "Track-Level Loudness by Genre",
       subtitle = "Violin + boxplot | 861 tracks",
       x = NULL, y = "Loudness (dB)")









The violin plot makes the distributional difference even clearer than the density plot above. Hard House tracks are tightly compressed into a narrow band around −6 dB, with very few outliers. The median sits noticeably higher than Minimal Tech House, whose distribution is wider and centred around −10 dB. The narrowness of the Hard House violin reflects a genre-wide mastering convention: every track is pushed to a similar loudness ceiling. Minimal Tech House allows for more variation, which is consistent with its emphasis on dynamics and textural subtlety rather than raw impact.

title: Week 8: Track-Level Features
text:
Chroma Features: East Bridge Romance
The chromagram is generated from NNLS Chroma features exported via Sonic Visualiser. Each row represents a pitch class (C through B), and each column a time frame. Intensity is mapped to colour using the viridis palette, producing a heatmap of harmonic activity over time.


Chromagram: East Bridge Romance (NNLS Chroma)
# east_bridge_chroma.csv has no header: 24 columns (bass + treble chroma from NNLS)
# We sum both sets of 12 into a single chroma profile per frame
pitch_names <- c("C","C#","D","Eb","E","F","F#","G","Ab","A","Bb","B")
ebr_raw <- read_csv("east_bridge_chroma.csv", col_names = FALSE, show_col_types = F)

# Bass chroma = columns 1-12, treble chroma = columns 13-24
bass <- ebr_raw[, 1:12]
treble <- ebr_raw[, 13:24]
colnames(bass) <- pitch_names
colnames(treble) <- pitch_names
ebr_chroma <- bass + treble
ebr_chroma$TIME <- seq(0, by = 0.023, length.out = nrow(ebr_chroma))

ebr_long <- ebr_chroma |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(pitch_names), names_to = "Pitch_Class", values_to = "Intensity") |>
  mutate(Pitch_Class = factor(Pitch_Class, levels = rev(pitch_names)))

ggplot(ebr_long, aes(x = TIME, y = Pitch_Class, fill = Intensity)) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "inferno", guide = "none") +
  theme_freq(11) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank()) +
  labs(title = "Chromagram: East Bridge Romance",
       subtitle = "NNLS Chroma features (bass + treble) | Hard House",
       x = "Time (s)", y = "")









The chromagram of East Bridge Romance shows repeated horizontal bands concentrated around a small number of pitch classes, revealing a loop-based harmonic structure typical of Hard House. Brighter areas align with the track’s drops, where multiple pitch classes activate simultaneously as layered synths and bass enter. Thinner, darker sections correspond to breakdowns where the arrangement strips back to percussion and atmosphere. What stands out is that formal structure in Hard House emerges not from harmonic development or modulation, but from textural contrast: the alternation between sparse and dense moments around a stable harmonic core.

title: Week 10: Tonal Centre
text: This section explores tonal structure through key estimation. A global key profile shows which pitch classes dominate across an entire track, while a keygram tracks how key estimates change over time. These methods are especially informative for EDM, where harmonic palettes are deliberately narrow and heavily reinforced.

title: Week 10: Tonal Centre
text: This section explores tonal structure through key estimation. A global key profile shows which pitch classes dominate across an entire track, while a keygram tracks how key estimates change over time. These methods are especially informative for EDM, where harmonic palettes are deliberately narrow and heavily reinforced.

title: Week 10: Tonal Centre
text:
Global Key Profile: Wood
The key profile is computed by averaging the NNLS Chroma intensities across the full track for each of the 12 pitch classes. The resulting bar chart acts as a tonal fingerprint, revealing which notes dominate the harmonic content.


Key profile: average chroma intensity per pitch class
# Load chroma data exported from Sonic Visualiser (NNLS Chroma plugin)
wood_data <- read_csv("wood.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Average each pitch class intensity across the full track duration
wood_avg <- wood_data |>
  select(-TIME) |>
  summarise(across(everything(), mean)) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Pitch_Class", values_to = "Intensity") |>
  mutate(Pitch_Class = factor(Pitch_Class,
    levels = c("C","C#","D","Eb","E","F","F#","G","Ab","A","Bb","B")))

# Bar chart showing which pitch classes dominate
ggplot(wood_avg, aes(x = Pitch_Class, y = Intensity, fill = Intensity)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(guide = "none", option = "plasma") +
  theme_freq(13) +
  labs(
    title = "Overall Key Profile: 'Wood'",
    subtitle = "Average pitch-class intensity across the full track",
    x = "Pitch Class", y = "Average Intensity"
  )









The bar chart shows the average intensity of each pitch class across the entire duration of Wood. A small number of pitch classes dominate clearly, while others are nearly absent. The strongest peaks appear on F, C, and G, with secondary emphasis on Bb and Eb. This pattern is consistent with an F minor or Ab major tonality (which share the same pitch class set), though the absence of strong thirds makes it difficult to distinguish major from minor with certainty. In EDM, where harmonic material is deliberately narrow and heavily reinforced through repetition, this profile acts as a compact fingerprint of tonal emphasis. The pronounced peaks connect directly to the loop-based patterns visible in the Week 9 chroma analysis: the same few notes that form the harmonic loop are the ones that accumulate the highest average intensity over time.

title: Week 10: Tonal Centre
text:
Keygram: Wood
The keygram computes a Euclidean distance between the chroma profile of each time window and the Krumhansl-Kessler key templates for all 24 major and minor keys. Darker cells indicate a closer match. This method reveals whether and when key changes occur.


Keygram: Krumhansl-Kessler key estimation over time
circshift<-function(v,n){if(n==0)v else c(tail(v,n),head(v,-n))}
major_key<-c(6.35,2.23,3.48,2.33,4.38,4.09,2.52,5.19,2.39,3.66,2.29,2.88)
minor_key<-c(6.33,2.68,3.52,5.38,2.60,3.53,2.54,4.75,3.98,2.69,3.34,3.17)
key_templates<-tribble(~name,~template,"Gb:maj",circshift(major_key,6),"Bb:min",circshift(minor_key,10),"Db:maj",circshift(major_key,1),"F:min",circshift(minor_key,5),"Ab:maj",circshift(major_key,8),"C:min",circshift(minor_key,0),"Eb:maj",circshift(major_key,3),"G:min",circshift(minor_key,7),"Bb:maj",circshift(major_key,10),"D:min",circshift(minor_key,2),"F:maj",circshift(major_key,5),"A:min",circshift(minor_key,9),"C:maj",circshift(major_key,0),"E:min",circshift(minor_key,4),"G:maj",circshift(major_key,7),"B:min",circshift(minor_key,11),"D:maj",circshift(major_key,2),"F#:min",circshift(minor_key,6),"A:maj",circshift(major_key,9),"C#:min",circshift(minor_key,1),"E:maj",circshift(major_key,4),"G#:min",circshift(minor_key,8),"B:maj",circshift(major_key,11),"D#:min",circshift(minor_key,3))
pitch_cols<-c("C","C#","D","Eb","E","F","F#","G","Ab","A","Bb","B")
tm<-do.call(rbind,key_templates$template);tm<-tm/rowSums(abs(tm))
ww<-wood_data|>mutate(window=(row_number()-1)%/%50)|>group_by(window)|>summarise(start=min(TIME),duration=max(TIME)-min(TIME),across(all_of(pitch_cols),mean),.groups="drop")
cm<-as.matrix(ww[,pitch_cols]);cn<-cm/(rowSums(abs(cm))+1e-10)
dm<-matrix(NA,nrow(cn),nrow(tm))
for(k in seq_len(nrow(tm))){d<-sweep(cn,2,tm[k,]);dm[,k]<-sqrt(rowSums(d^2))}
kl<-expand_grid(wi=seq_len(nrow(ww)),ki=seq_len(nrow(key_templates)))|>
  mutate(start=ww$start[wi],duration=ww$duration[wi],name=key_templates$name[ki],d=map2_dbl(wi,ki,\(w,k)dm[w,k]))|>
  mutate(name=factor(name,levels=key_templates$name))
ggplot(kl,aes(x=start+duration/2,width=duration,y=name,fill=d))+geom_tile()+
  scale_fill_viridis_c(guide="none")+theme_freq(11)+
  labs(title="Keygram: 'Wood'",subtitle="Krumhansl-Kessler key profile matching (darker = closer match)",x="Time (s)",y="")+
  theme(axis.text.y=element_text(size=7))









The keygram matches the chroma content of each time window against all 24 major and minor key templates using the Krumhansl-Kessler profiles. Darker horizontal bands indicate keys that consistently match well throughout the track. For Wood, the darkest bands correspond to Ab major and F minor, both of which remain stable across the entire duration with no visible modulation. This aligns with the key profile above and confirms that the track stays in a single tonal region throughout. The absence of any key change is consistent with the block structure observed in the Week 9 SSM and shows that compositional form in this genre relies on harmonic repetition rather than harmonic development. In traditional tonal music, key changes serve as a primary structural device to create tension and resolution, but EDM takes a fundamentally different approach: tension is created through textural buildup and release rather than harmonic motion.

title: Week 12: Classification & Clustering
text: This section tests whether Spotify’s audio features can reliably distinguish Minimal Tech House from Hard House using supervised classification (random forest) and unsupervised clustering (hierarchical). Together, these methods provide both a performance benchmark and an independent validation of the genre distinction.

title: Week 12: Classification & Clustering
text: This section tests whether Spotify’s audio features can reliably distinguish Minimal Tech House from Hard House using supervised classification (random forest) and unsupervised clustering (hierarchical). Together, these methods provide both a performance benchmark and an independent validation of the genre distinction.

title: Week 12: Classification & Clustering
text:
Confusion Matrix: Random Forest (10-fold CV)
A random forest classifier is trained using tidymodels with 10-fold stratified cross-validation. The confusion matrix heatmap shows how many tracks from each genre are correctly or incorrectly classified.


Confusion matrix: random forest 10-fold CV
forest_fit|>collect_predictions()|>conf_mat(truth=Genre,estimate=.pred_class)|>autoplot(type="heatmap")+
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option="plasma")+labs(title="Confusion Matrix: Random Forest (10-fold CV)")+
  theme_freq(13)+theme(panel.grid=element_blank(),legend.position="none")









The random forest classifier achieves a 10-fold cross-validated accuracy of 0.995, which shows that Minimal Tech House and Hard House are computationally distinguishable with high reliability. The confusion matrix shows that nearly all tracks are correctly classified, with only a handful of misclassifications. These errors likely correspond to boundary tracks that blend characteristics of both genres, consistent with the small overlap region visible in the Week 8 scatter plot.

title: Week 12: Classification & Clustering
text:
Feature Importance
Feature importance is extracted from the fitted random forest using the vip package. The importance score reflects how much each feature reduces impurity (Gini) across all decision trees. Higher values indicate features that contribute more to separating the genres.


Feature importance: impurity-based variable importance
importance_fit<-workflow()|>add_recipe(class_recipe)|>add_model(forest_model)|>fit(corpus_clean)
importance_fit|>extract_fit_parsnip()|>vip::vi()|>mutate(Variable=fct_reorder(Variable,Importance))|>
  ggplot(aes(x=Importance,y=Variable,fill=Importance))+geom_col()+scale_fill_viridis_c(guide="none",option="plasma")+
  theme_freq(12)+labs(title="Feature Importance: Random Forest",subtitle="Which Spotify features best separate the two genres?",x="Importance (impurity reduction)",y=NULL)









The feature importance ranking shows which audio features the classifier relies on most heavily. Tempo dominates, which aligns with the near-complete separation visible in the Week 11 histogram. Danceability, Energy, and Loudness follow closely, all features that directly relate to the physical experience of each genre. Features like Speechiness and Liveness contribute almost nothing to the classification, which makes sense for two purely electronic, instrumental genres where neither speech nor live performance characteristics play a role.

title: Week 12: Classification & Clustering
text:
Reduced Model: Top 5 Features
To test whether the full 10-feature model is necessary, a reduced random forest is trained using only the top 5 features from the importance ranking. This tests the robustness and parsimony of the genre distinction.


Reduced model: train with top 5 features only
reduced_recipe<-recipe(Genre~Tempo+Loudness+Energy+Danceability+Valence,data=corpus_clean)|>step_center(all_predictors())|>step_scale(all_predictors())
reduced_fit<-workflow()|>add_recipe(reduced_recipe)|>add_model(forest_model)|>fit_resamples(corpus_cv,control=control_resamples(save_pred=T))
reduced_accuracy<-reduced_fit|>collect_metrics()|>filter(.metric=="accuracy")|>pull(mean)|>round(3)




Confusion matrix: reduced model
reduced_fit|>collect_predictions()|>conf_mat(truth=Genre,estimate=.pred_class)|>autoplot(type="heatmap")+
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option="plasma")+labs(title="Reduced Model (Top 5 Features)")+
  theme_freq(13)+theme(panel.grid=element_blank(),legend.position="none")









The reduced model, using only Tempo, Loudness, Energy, Danceability, and Valence, achieves an accuracy of 0.994 compared to 0.995 with all ten features. The negligible difference confirms that the genre distinction is primarily encoded in a small set of features tied to tempo, loudness, and energy. The five removed features (Speechiness, Liveness, Instrumentalness, Acousticness, Duration) add almost no discriminatory power for this particular genre pair.

title: Week 12: Classification & Clustering
text:
Hierarchical Clustering: Dendrogram
As an unsupervised complement to the supervised classifier, hierarchical clustering is applied to a random sample of 60 tracks (30 per genre). Features are standardised, Euclidean distances are computed, and average-linkage clustering groups similar tracks together. The dendrogram is coloured by genre to assess whether the unsupervised structure aligns with the known labels.


Dendrogram: hierarchical clustering of 60 tracks
set.seed(123)
cs<-corpus_clean|>group_by(Genre)|>slice_sample(n=30)|>ungroup()|>mutate(label=paste0(str_trunc(`Track Name`,20)," [",if_else(Genre=="Hard House","HH","MT"),"]"))
cf<-cs|>select(label,Danceability,Energy,Loudness,Speechiness,Acousticness,Instrumentalness,Liveness,Valence,Tempo,`Duration (ms)`)|>column_to_rownames("label")
cl<-dist(scale(cf),method="euclidean")|>hclust(method="average");dd<-dendro_data(cl)
ldf<-dd$labels|>mutate(genre=if_else(str_detect(label,"\\[HH\\]"),"Hard House","Minimal Tech House"),col=if_else(genre=="Hard House","#ff2d55","#00d4ff"))
ggplot()+geom_segment(data=dd$segments,aes(x=x,y=y,xend=xend,yend=yend),colour="grey40",linewidth=0.4)+
  geom_text(data=ldf,aes(x=x,y=y-0.2,label=label,colour=col),hjust=1,size=2.3,angle=90)+
  scale_colour_identity()+scale_y_continuous(expand=expansion(mult=c(0.35,0.05)))+
  theme_freq(11)+theme(axis.text.x=element_blank(),axis.ticks.x=element_blank(),panel.grid=element_blank())+
  labs(title="Hierarchical Clustering: 60-Track Sample",subtitle="Average linkage | Euclidean distance | red = Hard House, cyan = Minimal Tech House",x=NULL,y="Distance")









The dendrogram provides an unsupervised validation of the supervised classification results. Using average-linkage hierarchical clustering on standardised features, the 60-track sample splits into two clearly distinct branches that align closely with the genre labels. Hard House tracks (red) group together on one side, while Minimal Tech House tracks (cyan) form a separate cluster. The fact that unsupervised clustering recovers the same genre boundary that the supervised classifier learned, without access to any labels, provides strong converging evidence that the distinction between these genres reflects genuine, measurable differences in audio features rather than merely a labelling convention.
